title: The stages of the path
hookLine: the step-by-step path from Atisha and Tsongkhapa

cards: Where do I actually start? Six days, six doors: the gray earth of Sakya, the path and its fruit, Gelug's virtuous way, the debate courtyard, Rime, Bon.

That's a lot of doors in one corridor, and somebody walking in fresh might reasonably ask: fine, but what comes first, and what comes after that? Tibetan teachers had an answer, laid out like a staircase.
It's called lamrim, the stages of the path, and the next days climb it one step at a time.

teach.b: First, the word. Lam is path, the same lam as in Lamdre. Rim means stages, or steps in a series.
Lamrim: the path in stages, each thing in its order. Second, Atisha, whom you met on day nine hundred thirty-six.
He was an Indian Buddhist master who traveled to Tibet, and there, tradition says, he was asked to write something short and clear for people confused by the many teachings arriving at once.
He wrote A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment.

teach.h: ATISHA'S LAMP: THREE KINDS OF PERSON.
teach.b: In it he sorts practitioners into three kinds of person: the one who looks for a good future in this round of lives, the one who wants to be free of the round altogether, and the one who wants to be free so that all beings can be free too.
Each is a step, and each includes the one below it. Third, Tsongkhapa, the founder of Gelug.
He opened Atisha's little lamp into a long, careful book, the Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path.
Teachers of Gelug and other schools still teach from lamrim texts, so a student can see where they are on the staircase and what comes next. Fourth, why stages help.
A beginner who leaps straight to the highest teaching often finds it floating with nothing under it. A staircase says: start with what this life is, then what it costs, then what you want for others.

teach.h: EACH STEP STANDS ON THE LAST.
teach.b: Each step is solid because of the one before, and the steps aren't left behind as you climb.
They're the floor you're standing on.

how: Tibetan Buddhist teachers, especially in the Gelug school, teach the lamrim in order, from the preciousness of human life through renunciation to compassion and wisdom, and students meditate on each stage in turn.

o: the final stage of the path, reached at the top

games.q: you're Atisha. people in Tibet are confused by all the teachings arriving at once. what do you give them?
o: the most advanced teaching, so they can skip ahead.
a short, clear lamp that lays the path out in order.
nothing; they should sort it out themselves.
games.why: tradition says Atisha wrote A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment, putting the teachings in order by kinds of person.

practice: Think of one thing you're trying to grow, patience, a skill, a practice, and name its steps in order: the very first one you can't skip, then the next, then one further on. Three or four is plenty, on paper or just in your head.
Then rest your attention on the first step, the one you're standing on now.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim. The stages of the path, from Atisha's Lamp to Tsongkhapa's Great Treatise: the whole way laid out step by step. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan: lam rim, the path (lam) in stages (rim).

carryVoice: Your line: step by step. A week of Tibetan schools ends here; the first stair comes tomorrow. See you then.
